```{r set_options, include = FALSE}
  collapse = TRUE,

  fig.align = "center"

```

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(phylograftR)
```

Grafting is stochastic, so a robust analysis may need **many grafted phylogenies**: N simulations, eventually crossed with P stochastic maps to apply attribute-based constraints (see `vignette("handle_uncertainty")`).
Each grafted phylogeny is **independent** from the others, so they can be computed **at the same time** on the different cores of your computer, using a **unique call** to one of the grafting functions.

This tutorial explains **how to run the grafting in parallel**, and **when it is worth it**. Parallel computation has a small cost (starting the workers, sending the data to them), so it is **not always faster**.
We present the results of a **benchmark** to help you decide, with the **expected gain** depending on the size of the backbone phylogeny, the number of grafted phylogenies, and the number of workers.

Here, we cover:

1. How to **set up** the parallel computation.
2. What is **run in parallel**, and why the output is the **same** as without parallelization.
3. The **design of the benchmark**, and the machine used.
4. The **results**: from which number of grafted phylogenies is it worth it, and which speed-up to expect.
5. **Larger backbones** (5,000 and 10,000 tips).
6. The **memory** needed.

Everything below applies in the same way to all grafting functions: `graft_missing_taxa()`, `graft_missing_clades()` and `graft_missing_taxa_and_clades()`.

## 1/ Set up the parallel computation

The parallel computation relies on the packages **`future`** and **`future.apply`**. They are **not installed with phylograftR**, so you must install them first.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages(c("future", "future.apply"))
```

phylograftR **does not manage the workers**: **you set a computation plan before the grafting**, and reset it afterwards.
The plan `multisession` starts separate R sessions (the *workers*), and works on all systems.

```{r plan, eval = FALSE}
# How many workers? You can use up to the number of physical cores of your computer, minus one or two to keep it responsive
parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE)

# Set the plan: Here, 4 workers
future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 4)
future::nbrOfWorkers()
#> [1] 4

# Run the grafting as usual
# The argument 'parallel = NULL' (default) uses the plan if one is set
grafted_phylo <- graft_missing_taxa(phy = toy_backbone,
                                    missing_taxa_list = toy_missing_taxa_list,
                                    nb_simulations = 100,
                                    seed = 1)

# Reset the plan when you are done, to free the workers
future::plan(future::sequential)
```

The argument `parallel` controls how the plan is used:

- `parallel = NULL` (default): the run is parallel **if a plan with several workers is set**, and sequential otherwise.
- `parallel = FALSE`: the plan is **ignored**, the run is sequential.
- `parallel = TRUE`: the plan is used, and the function **stops** if `future` is not installed or if no plan with several workers (i.e., with parallel computation) is set.

```{r parallel_true, eval = FALSE}
# No plan set: error
graft_missing_taxa(phy = toy_backbone, missing_taxa_list = toy_missing_taxa_list,
                   nb_simulations = 4, parallel = TRUE)
#> Error: 'parallel = TRUE' needs a 'future' plan with several workers, set before the call,
#> e.g., future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 4). Use 'parallel = FALSE' to run sequentially.
```

**Choosing the number of workers**: 

You can use up to the **number of physical cores of your computer**, minus one or two to keep your system responsive.
Keep in mind that **each worker is a full R session that needs its own memory**, so memory usage multiplies roughly linearly with the number of workers set  (see *Section 6* for estimates of memory usage).
There is also no point in having more workers than grafted phylogenies.

## 2/ What is run in parallel

Each **grafted phylogeny** is one **independent task**: one simulation (one seed) for one stochastic map.
With `P` maps and `nb_simulations = N`, all the `P x N` tasks are **shared evenly across the workers**. There is no need to loop over the maps yourself.

```{r tasks, eval = FALSE}
# 10 stochastic maps x 5 simulations = 50 tasks, shared among the workers
future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 4)
grafted_phylo_par <- graft_missing_taxa(phy = toy_backbone,
                                        missing_taxa_list = taxa_colors, # See `vignette("handle_uncertainty")`
                                        simmap = toy_multiSimmap,
                                        nb_simulations = 5,
                                        seed = 1)
future::plan(future::sequential)
```

### The output is the same as in a sequential run

The **seed system** is not affected by the parallelization: each grafted phylogeny uses its own seed, derived from `seed` (see `vignette("handle_uncertainty")`).
The output is thus **exactly the same** with or without parallelization, whatever the number of workers.

```{r identical, eval = FALSE}

# Run the same example without a parallel plan = sequentially
grafted_phylo_seq <- graft_missing_taxa(phy = toy_backbone,
                                        missing_taxa_list = taxa_colors,
                                        simmap = toy_multiSimmap,
                                        nb_simulations = 5,
                                        seed = 1,
                                        parallel = FALSE) # Ignore the plan

# Compare outputs
identical(grafted_phylo_seq, grafted_phylo_par)
#> [1] TRUE
```

The format and names of the outputs are the same too (here: a list of 10 `multiPhylo` named `map_1`, `map_2`, ...). Everything you learn in `vignette("handle_uncertainty")` applies.

The only difference: **messages and warnings** raised in the workers are **relayed to your session once the tasks are collected**, so they appear after the run, not live.
With `verbose = TRUE`, one line is printed when each simulation is done.

## 3/ Benchmark: design and machine

We benchmarked the computation time of the grafting, sequential and parallel, to find from which size of backbone and number of grafted phylogenies the parallelization pays off.

**Machine**: Intel Xeon W-2255 (3.7 GHz), 10 physical cores (20 threads).

**Configurations**:

- **Backbones**: random coalescent trees of **100, 500, 1000, 5,000 and 10,000 tips**.
- **Taxa to graft**: **as many as tips** for 100, 500 and 1000 tips (e.g., 1000 taxa on a backbone of 1000 tips), which is a **demanding case**, as the time of a grafting depends mostly on the number of taxa to graft. For larger phylogenies, we used a more realistic scenario with **20% of the tips** to graft for 5,000 and 10,000 tips (1,000 and 2,000 taxa).
- **Taxa distribution**: taxa spread over a few target clades, with a **broken stick distribution** of the number of taxa per clade (a few large groups of taxa, and many small ones, as in a taxonomy).
- **Number of simulations**: 10, 100 and 1000 simulations, without stochastic maps: the final number of grafted phylogenies equals the number of simulations.
- **Number of workers for parallelization**: 2, 4 and 10 workers, with the plan `future::multisession`. The times include the set-up of the workers, as when you set the plan just before the grafting.

Both **methods**, `"uniform"` and `"BD_clades"` have the **same cost** when using only simulations (i.e., no stochastic maps for attribute-based constraints), as the birth-death model is fitted only once per target clade.


### Fixed costs and time of one task

Setting up the workers, loading phylograftR in each of them, and sending the data has a **fixed cost**, paid once per plan. It **increases with the number of workers**:

| Workers | Set-up time |
|:---|:---|
| 2 | about 14 s |
| 4 | about 18 s |
| 10 | about 32 s |

Keep the plan set across several grafting calls to **pay this cost only once**.

The time of one task, i.e., **one grafted phylogeny**, grows with the size of the backbone and the number of taxa to graft:

| Backbone | Taxa to graft | One grafted phylogeny (sequential) |
|:---|---:|:---|
| 100 tips | 100 | 0.5 s |
| 500 tips | 500 | 11 s |
| 1000 tips | 1000 | 41 s |
| 5,000 tips | 1,000 | 3 min |
| 10,000 tips | 2,000 | 13 min |

## 4/ Results: when does parallel pay off?

### Benchmark results

The table gives the time of the runs for all combinations of backbone and number of simulations (`N`), sequential and with 2, 4 and 10 workers, with the **speed-up** in brackets (sequential time / parallel time).
A speed-up below 1 means that the parallel run is **slower**.

| Backbone | Taxa to graft | Simulations (N) | Sequential | 2 workers | 4 workers | 10 workers |
|:---|---:|---:|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 100 tips | 100 | 10 | 5 s | 19 s (x0.3) | 23 s (x0.2) | 33 s (x0.1) |
| 100 tips | 100 | 100 | 49 s | 41 s (x1.2) | 32 s (x1.5) | 38 s (x1.3) |
| 100 tips | 100 | 1000 | 8.7 min | 4.5 min (x1.9) | 2.9 min (x3.0) | 90 s (x5.5) |
| 500 tips | 500 | 10 | 1.8 min | 1.1 min (x1.6) | 53 s (x2.0) | 44 s (x2.5) |
| 500 tips | 500 | 100 | 18 min | 9 min (x2.0) | 5 min (x3.5) | 3 min (x7.2) |
| 500 tips | 500 | 1000 | 3.0 h | 1.5 h (x2.0) | 50 min (x3.6) | 20 min (x8.9) |
| 1,000 tips | 1,000 | 10 | 6.8 min | 3.4 min (x2.0) | 2.4 min (x2.9) | 73 s (x5.5) |
| 1,000 tips | 1,000 | 100 | 1.1 h | 34 min (x2.0) | 17 min (x3.9) | 7 min (x9.2) |
| 1,000 tips | 1,000 | 1000 | 11.3 h | 5.6 h (x2.0) | 2.9 h (x4.0) | 1.1 h (x9.8) |
| 5,000 tips | 1,000 | 10 | 33 min | 17 min (x2.0) | 10 min (x3.2) | 4 min (x8.5) |
| 5,000 tips | 1,000 | 100 | 5.6 h | 2.8 h (x2.0) | 1.4 h (x3.9) | 34 min (x9.7) |
| 5,000 tips | 1,000 | 1000 | 2 days | 27.8 h (x2.0) | 14.0 h (x4.0) | 5.6 h (x9.9) |
| 10,000 tips | 2,000 | 10 | 2.2 h | 1.1 h (x2.0) | 40 min (x3.3) | 14 min (x9.5) |
| 10,000 tips | 2,000 | 100 | 21.9 h | 11.0 h (x2.0) | 5.5 h (x4.0) | 2.2 h (x9.9) |
| 10,000 tips | 2,000 | 1000 | 9 days | 5 days (x2.0) | 2 days (x4.0) | 22.2 h (x9.9) |

Three things stand out:

1. On a **small backbone (100 tips) with few simulations**, the parallel run is **slower**: the set-up of the workers takes more time than the sequential run.
2. From **500 tips**, the gain is clear even with 10 simulations: about **x2 with 2 workers and x2 to x3 with 4 workers**.
3. When each grafted phylogeny takes **10 seconds or more**, the gain is **close to the number of workers**.

### Expected gain

We model the expected gain from the results of the benchmark, accounting for the **fixed cost of setting up the workers**, which increases with the number of workers, and the **time of one task**.
The figure shows the expected speed-up as a function of the number of grafted phylogenies (`P x N`), for 2, 4 and 10 workers. The plain red line stands at X1 (even time cost for sequential and parallel computing), thus all cases above this line are cases when **parallel computation offers a gain**.

```{r model_plot, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
# Parameters estimated on the benchmark machine
backbones <- data.frame(tips = c(100, 500, 1000),
                        time_one = c(0.49, 10.9, 40.6),        # Seconds per grafted phylogeny (sequential)
                        overhead = c(0.17, 0.09, 0.01))        # Relative overhead of the parallel run
fixed_cost <- c("2" = 13.5, "4" = 18.2, "10" = 32.3)           # Seconds to set up the workers

speed_up <- function (N, time_one, workers, overhead)
{
  overhead <- if (workers == 2) 0 else overhead
  time_par <- fixed_cost[as.character(workers)] + (N / workers) * time_one * (1 + overhead)
  return(N * time_one / time_par)
}

N_grid <- exp(seq(log(4), log(1000), length.out = 150))
cols <- c("100" = "#1B9E77", "500" = "#D95F02", "1000" = "dodgerblue")
ltys <- c("2" = 3, "4" = 2, "10" = 1)

plot(NA, xlim = c(4, 1000), ylim = c(0, 10.5), log = "x",
     xlab = "Number of grafted phylogenies (P x N)", ylab = "Speed-up (sequential time / parallel time)")
abline(h = 1, lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = "red")
for (i in seq_len(nrow(backbones)))
{
  b <- backbones[i, ]
  for (W in c(2, 4, 10))
  {
    lines(N_grid, sapply(N_grid, speed_up, time_one = b$time_one, workers = W, overhead = b$overhead),
          col = cols[as.character(b$tips)], lty = ltys[as.character(W)], lwd = 2)
  }
}

legend("topleft", legend = c("100 tips", "500 tips", "1000 tips", "2 workers", "4 workers", "10 workers"),
       col = c(cols, rep("grey30", 3)), lty = c(1, 1, 1, 3, 2, 1), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

### From which number of grafted phylogenies is it worth it?

The take-home messages are:

- **Small backbones (about 100 tips or less, or few taxa to graft)**: a grafted phylogeny is fast, so the parallelization only pays off for **hundreds of grafted phylogenies**. Under 50 grafted phylogenies, **do not bother**.
- **Backbones of 500 tips or more**: it pays off from **about 10 grafted phylogenies**. Use it by default.
- When the backbone phylogeny and/or the numebr of tips to graft are large, and the run lasts several minutes or more, **the expected gain is about the number of workers** (x2 with 2 workers, x3.5 to x4 with 4 workers, up to x9 or x10 with 10 workers). Below that, the fixed cost of setting up the workers limits the gain.

As a **rule of thumb**: use parallel computation when the **sequential run would last more than a minute or two**.
You can get an estimate by timing one grafted phylogeny:

```{r time_one, eval = FALSE}
# Time of one grafted phylogeny (sequential), including the preparation of the grafting
time_one <- system.time(graft_missing_taxa(phy = my_backbone,
                                           missing_taxa_list = my_missing_taxa_list,
                                           simmap = my_simmap[[1]], # Optional: a single map
                                           nb_simulations = 1, seed = 1,
                                           parallel = FALSE))["elapsed"]

# Expected sequential time of the full run, in minutes
time_one * P * N / 60
```

### With stochastic maps

The benchmark above grafts the taxa **without stochastic maps**. With a simmap, each grafted phylogeny takes **roughly 10% to 30% longer**, as the states of the branches must be tracked and matched with the allowed states of each taxon.
The **gain from parallel computation and the rules of thumb are therefore about the same**: multiply the times of the tables by about 1.2.

One exception: with `"BD_clades"`, the time can be **several times longer** when the allowed states leave only a **narrow part of the time window** with available branches. The divergence ages drawn from the birth-death model then often fall where no branch is in an allowed state, and have to be **redrawn**, again and again (see `max_age_redraws`). The time then varies a lot among simulations (up to x10 longer when the number of draws needed is close to 1,000). It can affect the overall time needed, but this time cost applies only for maps that have a small portion of valid branches available (`min_valid_fraction`).
You can inspect if such issue, and for which maps, is likely to arrive beforehand using the `check_grafting_plan()` function.

## 5/ Larger backbones (5,000 and 10,000 tips)

Backbones of **thousands of tips** are realistic for phylograftR, but then it is unlikely that the number of taxa to graft equals the number of tips. The **cost of a grafting depends much more on the number of taxa to graft than on the number of tips**:
on a backbone of 1000 tips, grafting 100, 250, 500 and 1000 taxa takes about 7%, 19%, 40% and 100% of the time needed for 1000 taxa, so the time grows **slightly faster than linearly** with the number of taxa.

We therefore benchmarked backbones of 5,000 and 10,000 tips with **20% of missing taxa** (1,000 and 2,000 taxa): see the latest rows of the table in *Section 4*.

At this scale, **parallel computation is not optional**. A single grafted phylogeny takes about 3 minutes (5,000 tips) to about 13 minutes (10,000 tips), so a set of 100 grafted phylogenies would last about 5 hours to about 22 hours sequentially.
The fixed cost of setting up the workers is negligible, and the speed-up is close to the number of workers.

## 6/ Memory needed

Each worker is a **separate R session**, with its own copy of the backbone and of the objects needed for the grafting. The **memory used is therefore about `(1 + number of workers)` times the memory of one R session** running one grafting.
The table gives the **approximate peak memory of all the R sessions**:

| Run | 100 to 1000 tips | 5,000 tips | 10,000 tips |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Sequential | 0.3 GB | 0.3 GB | 0.7 GB |
| 2 workers | 0.8 GB | 0.9 GB | 1.5 GB |
| 4 workers | 1.4 GB | 1.5 GB | 2.5 GB |
| 10 workers | 3 GB | 3.5 GB | 5.5 GB |

The grafted phylogenies themselves are small (0.06 MB for 100 tips, 0.6 MB for 1000 tips with as many taxa grafted), so sets of 1000 grafted phylogenies add less than 1 GB in your main session.

Memory is thus **not a limiting factor on a recent computer**. If you are short of memory, check the memory of a single grafting (run one simulation sequentially and look at the memory used by the R session in the task manager of your system), make sure that `(1 + workers) x this value` fits in your RAM, and **reduce the number of workers** if needed: the speed-up decreases, but the run completes.
